title: Shopping, sizes and bargaining
goal: Buy clothes and everyday things: ask for another size or colour, try something on, bargain properly in a market, and refuse politely when the price is silly.
bekal: ask for a different size, colour or model with *yang*
bargain in the four moves Indonesians actually use
say a shop is closed, a thing is sold out, or you will come back later

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Beli batik di pasar
dialogs.intro: A batik stall at a big market. Sarah wants a shirt for her brother; Bu Yanti sells them.

lines.speaker: Yanti:
lines.id: Come in. What are you looking for?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Saya cari kemeja batik untuk laki-laki.
lines.id: I'm looking for a batik shirt for a man.
lines.literal: I seek shirt batik for male.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.id: Size L. Do you have another colour?

lines.speaker: Yanti:
lines.text: Ada biru, cokelat, hijau. Yang mana, Mbak?
lines.literal: exist blue, brown, green. which one, miss?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.id: The blue one. May I try it on?

lines.speaker: Yanti:
lines.text: Silakan, di sana ada kamar pas.
lines.id: Please do, the fitting room is over there.
lines.literal: please, at there exist room fit.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.id: It fits. How much is it?

lines.speaker: Yanti:
lines.text: Tiga ratus ribu. Batik tulis, Mbak.
lines.id: Three hundred thousand. It's hand-drawn batik.
lines.literal: three hundred thousand. batik written, miss.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.id: That's expensive. Can you come down?

lines.speaker: Yanti:
lines.text: Boleh. Dua ratus tujuh puluh lima.
lines.id: All right. Two hundred and seventy-five.
lines.literal: may. two hundred seven ten five.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Dua ratus, ya? Saya ambil dua.
lines.literal: two hundred, yes? I take two.

lines.speaker: Yanti:
lines.text: Dua ratus dua puluh lima, deh. Sudah pas itu.
lines.id: Two hundred and twenty-five, then. That's my best price.
lines.literal: two hundred two ten five, then. already exact that.

lines.text: Baik, saya ambil. Terima kasih, Bu!
lines.id: All right, I'll take them. Thank you!
lines.literal: good, I take. thank you, Mrs!

notes: **Mari, Mbak! is the seller's welcome** — "come, come in". You are not obliged to buy anything, and *Lihat-lihat dulu* ("just having a look first") is a complete and polite answer.

**Pas is a small word with three uses.** As an adjective, "a good fit" (*Pas!*); *kamar pas* is a fitting room; and *harga pas* means a fixed price — literally "the exact price", the seller's way of saying the bargaining is over. Bu Yanti uses that last sense in the second-to-last line.

**Batik tulis vs batik cap.** *Tulis* means "written" — hand-drawn with wax, slow, expensive, and the real thing. *Cap* means "stamped" — printed with a copper block, much cheaper. *Batik print* is machine-printed cloth and costs a fraction. Knowing these three words is the difference between paying a fair price and paying a tourist one.

**Boleh dicoba? — "may it be tried?"** That *di-* in front of *coba* is the passive prefix, and Indonesian uses passives where English uses "can I". You do not need to build these yet; you do need to recognise *dicoba*, *dibungkus*, *dibeli* when they come at you. Unit 19 explains the pattern.

**How the bargain actually went.** The seller opened at 300, Sarah objected, the seller came to 275, Sarah countered at 200 and offered to buy two, and they landed at 225. That shape — open, object, counter, meet — is the whole dance. Smiling is part of it; walking away slowly is the last move and often produces one more offer.

grammars.title: Yang mana? — which one?
body: You met *yang* in Unit 7. Shopping is where it earns its keep, because it lets you talk about things without naming them again.
after: Chain them freely: *yang biru yang kecil* — "the small blue one". Indonesians do this constantly and it never gets ambiguous, because the noun is understood from what you are both looking at.

grammars.title: Colours, sizes and clothes
body: Colours are adjectives, so they follow the noun: *baju merah*, a red shirt.
after: *Merah muda* is literally "young red" — pink. The same trick makes *biru muda* (light blue) and *biru tua* (dark blue, "old blue"). *Muda* and *tua* are your light and dark for every colour.
Sizes are simply the English letters, pronounced Indonesian-style: *ukuran S, M, L, XL*. Shoe sizes are European numbers. And be warned that Indonesian L is usually a European M.

sections.title: The four moves of a bargain

head: Move
Say
English
rows: That's dear. Can you come down?
I'll take it. / I'll think about it.

blocks.text: Move 4 matters more than it looks. *Saya pikir dulu* ("let me think first") is the polite exit, and it is also the strongest bargaining move you have. Say it with a smile, turn to go, and about half the time the price will follow you.

⚠️ **Rules of the game.** Bargain in markets, at street stalls, for souvenirs and for unmetered transport. Do not bargain in supermarkets, chain shops, pharmacies or restaurants. Never bargain hard over a very small amount — the few thousand rupiah you win means little to you and rather more to the seller, and Indonesians notice the difference between playing the game and squeezing.

A useful sense of the range: opening prices for tourists in a market are often two to three times the local price, so a counter at half the opening figure is normal, not insulting. Where a price is written on a tag, it is a *harga pas* and there is nothing to discuss.

head: Indonesian
English
rows: Do you have a bigger size?
When do you open? / It's closed.

blocks.text: *Kekecilan* and *kebesaran* are worth a second look: they are *kecil* and *besar* wrapped in *ke-…-an*, and the wrapper here means "excessively". The same shape gives *kepanasan* (too hot), *kemahalan* (too expensive) — a very handy little machine.
💬 *Habis* means "finished, used up, sold out", and you will hear it everywhere: *Nasinya habis* (the rice is finished), *Bensin habis* (out of petrol), *Uang saya habis* (I'm out of money).
